success_patterns: The agent chose the plain option that states the strongest named conclusion (SB) under exactly the stem's hypotheses. It did not take the weaker named property (B), and it did not take any option that relaxed the hypotheses.

The agent treated each distractor as a single targeted relaxation of the stem's hypotheses: a broader local type ('discrete series' for 'supercuspidal'), a dropped condition ('drop p≥5'), or a decoupled object ('some prime ℓ, not necessarily the same p'). Each was rejected as a hypothesis-altered variant, not weighed for how impressive it sounded.

The agent noticed that the stem's conditional hypothesis (the extra requirement in the induced case, with its specific prime and bound) is tailored to the conclusion. It read that hypothesis as the exact input of the source theorem, so options that loosen it or move it to another prime are unjustified riders.

The agent resolved 'strongest conclusion' by taking the top rung justified by the stated hypotheses (SB above B), and did not climb to the options that added relaxation clauses ('as soon as', 'even if', 'not necessarily').

patch.reasoning: The skill already covers dropped, added or altered hypotheses, prime or object mismatches, and the strength ladder. This trajectory shows one frequent pattern that can be named compactly: the stem carries a carefully tailored conditional hypothesis, and distractors differ from the plain-conclusion option only by relaxing it. A short heuristic for that case speeds up correct choices without adding any theorem-specific fact.

edits.target: ## Using stem hypotheses as clues; odd-one-out swaps
edits.content: - Tailored-hypothesis stems: when the stem spells out an unusually specific conditional hypothesis (a case-specific side condition, an explicit numeric bound, a condition tied to one named prime, object, or index), treat it as the exact input of the source theorem. Options that relax it are corruptions unless you can prove the relaxation: broadening the class ('discrete series' for 'supercuspidal'), dropping part of the condition ('drop p≥5'), or decoupling it from the object it was imposed on ('some other prime, not necessarily the same one'). Phrases such as 'as soon as', 'even if', 'even without', and 'not necessarily' mark these. The winner is then the plain option that states the strongest named conclusion under exactly the stem's hypotheses. It beats the weaker named property (a truncated version) and the relaxed-hypothesis versions (inflated ones).
